newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China diesel imports seen still strong in Q2.
newsitem.headline: China diesel imports seen still strong in Q2.

text.p: China is expected to continue strong imports of diesel in the second quarter of this year, although the amount could be slightly lower than in the first quarter, oil industry sources said on Wednesday.

China's rapid economic expansion is fuelling the need for diesel imports as China's refineries can not keep pace with demand and some halts for maintenance at Chinese refineries in the second quarter should also keep imports up, they said.
Customs data showed China imported 2.06 million tonnes of diesel in the first quarter of 1997, nearly half of the 4.6 million tonnes it imported in the whole 1996.

Chinese oil companies stopped ordering diesel on international markets in late 1996 as prices were much higher than those set by China's inflation-wary bureaucrats, sending annual imports plunging some 23 percent from a year earlier.
China imported six million tonnes of diesel in 1995, 0.8 percent lower than in 1994.
China's diesel imports are expected to swell back to pre-1996 levels, with Chinese traders estimating monthly imports of 600-700,000 tonnes in 1997.

Demand from agriculture, transportation, factories as well as power stations is expected to continue growing in line with China's open economic policy, said a source with China's state trader Sinochem in Beijing.
"The second quarter imports should remain steady and strong though not as big as in the first quarter," said a trader with a Singapore firm which handles trade with China.
"Imports should remain quite steady throughout this year," the source said.
The huge first quarter imports were attributed to the diesel supply shortage in late 1996. "The negative margins made the inventory level very low at that time," said one trader in Hong Kong.
China needs to maintain the current import level to meet domestic deamnd and while some of its refineries are still down in the second quarter, the trader said.
"The actual (first quarter) amount must be higher than the customs data," said a trader with a Chinese state oil firm in Singapore.

"The total imports could be as much as three million tonnes in the first quarter if you add those did not go through the customs," the trader said, noting diesel was smuggled into southeast China from Hong Kong.

Due to soaring diesel imports, some Chinese refiners urged the government to halt import licences at the end of the first quarter, but customs figures showed the calls had little impact, traders said.
"The huge imports in the first quarter were exceptional. There shouldn't be such demand in the second quarter," one trader in Singapore said.
As some Chinese refineries have just restarted in late April after scheduled maintenance halts and some are still partly shut down, the need for imported diesel is still there, traders said.

China's Guangzhou Refinery, which has a capacity of up to 140,000 bpd, and the 100,000-bpd Dalian West Pacific Petroleum Company both restarted production at the end of April after scheduled maintenance.
The Fujian refinery is expected to restart soon.
In April alone, China imported at least 750,000 tonnes of diesel from South Korea and would continue to boost imports from its neighbour in future, Chinese importers said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65 870-3571)
